children: By Nate Raymond

A federal judge on Thursday expressed skepticism that President Donald Trump's administration should be allowed to proceed with a lawsuit seeking to force Harvard University to turn over records for an investigation into whether it continues to consider race in its student admissions process.

US District Judge Myong Joun during a hearing in Boston questioned whether the administration followed the proper procedures before filing the lawsuit, which Harvard says is part of Trump's broader campaign against the Ivy League school.

The Justice Department sued Harvard in February, arguing the university was not complying with investigations into whether it is following the US Supreme Court's 2023 ruling rejecting race-conscious admissions programs used to boost enrollment of minority students.

Deputy Assistant Attorney General Jeffrey Morrison told Joun that the Justice Department and Department of Education need years of applicant-level admissions data to determine whether race remains a factor in Harvard's admissions decisions.
"If Harvard willing to negotiate, we would certainly negotiate on how broad it is," he said.
But Joun suggested that offer came too late, noting Harvard's argument that the government sued without first taking legally required steps aimed at securing the university's voluntary compliance.
"That doesn't appear to be a willingness to negotiate," said Joun, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden. "It's just an ultimatum."

Harvard has been a central target of the administration's effort to leverage federal funding and the power of the government to force changes at universities that Trump says are dominated by "radical left" ideologies.

The university's lawyers contend the case was filed to retaliate against Harvard for refusing demands that it overhaul its governance, hiring and academic programs to align with the administration's agenda.

The university has already secured rulings from other judges rejecting the administration's efforts to terminate over $2 billion in grants, block the school from hosting international students and sue it for allegedly failing to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment.

Harvard's attorneys say the lawsuit before Joun was filed only after Trump announced in early February that he was ending settlement talks and wanted $1 billion in damages from Harvard, which had "been, for a long time, behaving very badly."
"The government needed another hammer against Harvard," said Stuart Delery, Harvard's lawyer.

He said Harvard had already provided sufficient records and data for the government to assess its compliance with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bars racial discrimination in education programs.
Yet he said the administration was now demanding years of sensitive admissions data on thousands of high school students who applied for admission to Harvard.
"This is information that students and families expect — and the law expects — Harvard to safeguard," he said.
The case is United States v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, No. 26-cv-10844.
For the United States: Jeffrey Morrison of the US Department of Justice
For Harvard: Stuart Delery of Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher
Judge questions whether administration followed required steps before suing Harvard
Justice Department says it needs years of applicant-level data to assess Harvard admissions
Harvard says administration seeks sensitive data on thousands of high school applicants
